# Job 9 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview of the Chapter

Job 9 is Job's reply to Bildad (who had spoken in ch. 8). Job agrees with Bildad's general premise that God is just and mighty, but he turns it in a devastating direction: precisely *because* God is so mighty, a mortal has no chance of establishing his righteousness before Him. The chapter is structured as a legal disputation — Job imagines a court case between himself and God and concludes that the contest is hopelessly unequal. The chapter peaks at vv. 32–33 with the cry for a "daysman" (mediator/arbitrator).

- **Gill:** "This and the following chapter contain Job's answer to Bildad… he asserts the strict justice of God; which is such, that no man can be just in his sight." [Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/9.htm)
- **Pulpit Commentary:** "Job, in answer to Bildad, admits the truth of his arguments, but declines to attempt the justification which can alone entitle him to accept the favourable side of Bildad's alternative. Man cannot absolutely justify himself before God." [Pulpit](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/9.htm)
- **Nicoll (Expositor's Bible):** "It is with an infinitely sad restatement of what God has been made to appear to him by Bildad's speech that Job begins his reply." [Expositor's Bible](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/job-9.html)
- **Constable:** "Job began his response to Bildad by acknowledging that much of what his friends had said was true (Job 9:2). … God appeared to Job to be acting arbitrarily and capriciously." [Constable](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/job-9.html)

---

## v. 1: "Then Job answered:"

**Traditional reading:** Job begins his reply without directly mentioning Bildad's harsh words, entering straight into the theological argument.

- **Gill:** "Without taking notice of Bildad's harsh expressions and severe censures, or his unfriendliness to him; he enters directly into the argument, grants some things, confutes others, and defends himself and his conduct." [Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/9.htm)

---

## v. 2: "Yes, I know that it is so, but how can a mortal be righteous before God?"

**Traditional reading:** Job concedes Bildad's general point — God does not pervert justice (Job 8:3). But the practical question remains: if even Job, a man of integrity, cannot be considered righteous enough to escape suffering, then who can? The Hebrew word for "mortal" is *enosh*, emphasising human frailty.

- **Gill:** "Job was a man of great natural parts and capacity … he knew that God was just and holy in all his ways and works … but then the matter is: how should man be just with God? … a man can only be just with God through the imputation of the righteousness of Christ." [Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/9.htm)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** "Job's question here concerns the first aspect of righteousness [relative, among men] … 'If I have not been righteous enough to escape the judgment of God, then who can be?' Yet in the ultimate sense, Job's question is the most important question in the world. How can a man find God's approval?" [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-9/)
- **Pulpit Commentary:** "How should man be just with God? … Apart from any knowledge of the doctrine of original or inherited sin, each man feels, deep in his heart, that he is sinful … 'But for the grace of God, there goes John Bradford!'" [Pulpit](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/9.htm)
- **Constable:** "This is not a question about salvation ('How may I be justified?') but about vindication ('How can I be declared innocent?')." [Constable](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/job-9.html)
- **Geneva Study Bible:** "Job here answers Eliphaz and Bildad's oration, touching the justice of God, and his innocency, confessing God to be infinite in justice and man to be nothing in respect." [Geneva](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gsb/job-9.html)
- **Preacher's Homiletical:** "The language suggests the impossibility of fallen man establishing his righteousness with God." [Preacher's Homiletical](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/job-9.html)
- **James Smith (Precept Austin):** "How is man's iniquity to be put away, and the guilt of his sin cleansed? … This question has been fully answered by God Himself … in the gift and sufferings of Jesus Christ His Son." [Smith](https://www.preceptaustin.org/job-commentary-james-smith)

---

## v. 3: "If one wished to contend with God, he could not answer Him one time out of a thousand."

**Traditional reading:** The word "contend" (Hebrew *rib*) is a legal term meaning to bring a lawsuit. If a man dared to take God to court, he could not answer even one charge out of a thousand that God might bring against him — because every human is guilty of countless sins.

- **Gill:** "If God will contend with man … enter into a controversy with him, litigate and dispute the point in law … man cannot answer … for one sin of a thousand he has committed." [Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/9.htm)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** "'Here the word contend is the technical term for conducting a law-suit' (Andersen)." [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-9/)
- **Geneva:** "Of a thousand things, which God could lay to his charge, man cannot answer him one." [Geneva](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gsb/job-9.html)
- **Pulpit:** "Of the charges which God might in his omniscience bring against him, he could not make a satisfactory reply to one in a thousand." [Pulpit](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/9.htm)

---

## v. 4: "God is wise in heart and mighty in strength. Who has resisted Him and prospered?"

**Traditional reading:** Job sets forth the inequality of the contest: God's wisdom and power are absolute; no one who has hardened himself against God has ever succeeded.

- **Gill:** "He is the only, and the all wise God; his understanding is infinite … he is the Almighty … who hath hardened himself against him, and hath prospered? either by behaving proudly … as Pharaoh, Sennacherib, and others." [Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/9.htm)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** "Job agreed with the basic premise of Bildad, that one is never blessed by hardening one's self against God. Yet Job did not think that this principle applied to himself in this situation." [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-9/)
- **Preacher's Homiletical:** "Men harden themselves against God … by stout and scornful words … by stout and presumptuous deeds." [Preacher's Homiletical](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/job-9.html)

---

## v. 5: "He moves mountains without their knowledge and overturns them in His anger."

**Traditional reading:** An illustration of God's irresistible power in nature — perhaps referring to earthquakes or volcanic activity. Mountains, the most stable and immovable features of the landscape, are moved by God without their "knowing" (either they are unaware, or men in them are unaware).

- **Gill:** "This and what follow are instances of the power of God … either literally … or figuratively, of kingdoms and mighty kings … comparable to mountains for their height and strength, who yet are removed by God at his pleasure." [Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/9.htm)

---

## v. 6: "He shakes the earth from its place, so that its foundations tremble."

**Traditional reading:** A further example of God's power in earthquakes. Some see a reference to the Flood or to the final judgment.

- **Gill:** "Can do it, and will do it at the last day, when it shall be utterly broken down … and this may also refer to the time of the flood." [Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/9.htm)

---

## v. 7: "He commands the sun not to shine; He seals off the stars."

**Traditional reading:** God controls the heavenly bodies absolutely. Some commentators link this to the darkness at the Flood, the plague of darkness in Egypt, or simply to cloud cover and eclipses.

- **Gill:** "Either he could do it if he would, by a word speaking … or else the sense is, it rises not at any other time and place but when and where he commands it … some think this respects the three days' darkness in Egypt … or rather it refers to the general flood." [Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/9.htm)

---

## v. 8: "He alone stretches out the heavens and treads on the waves of the sea."

**Traditional reading:** God's sole and unaided creative and governing power. "Treads on the waves" is a striking image of dominion over the chaotic sea — an image later fulfilled literally when Jesus walked on water.

- **Gill:** "Which alone spreadeth out the heavens … without the help of any creature, angels or men … and treadeth upon the waves of the sea … he rules their raging, stills their noise, and makes them smooth, calm, and quiet." [Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/9.htm)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** "Mason demonstrates … We read that God treads on the waves of the sea; Jesus walks on the water." [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-9/)
- **Note on textual variant:** There is a Masoretic reading of "high places of the cloud" instead of "waves of the sea" (noted by Vatablus, cited in Gill).

---

## v. 9: "He is the Maker of the Bear and Orion, of the Pleiades and the constellations of the south."

**Traditional reading:** God is the Creator of the constellations. The Bear (Arcturus/Great Bear) represents the northern sky, Orion the southern, the Pleiades the east, and "the chambers of the south" the hidden constellations below the southern horizon.

- **Ellicott:** "This shows us that in the time of this writer … his fellow-countrymen had attained to such knowledge of astronomy as is here implied in the specific names of definite constellations. The Great Bear is the glory of the northern hemisphere, Orion of the southern sky, and the Pleiades of the east; the chambers of the north are the unknown and unexplored regions." [Ellicott](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/9.htm)
- **Gill:** "Which maketh Arcturus … by which is meant not a single star, but a collection of stars … a constellation … these three divide the whole year." [Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/9.htm)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** "'Chambers of the south' — 'The most remote, hidden, and secret parts of the south; so called, because the stars which are under the southern pole are hidden from us, and are enclosed and lodged as in a chamber' (Trapp)." [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-9/)
- **Geneva:** "These are the names of certain stars by which he means that all stars both known and unknown are at his appointment." [Geneva](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gsb/job-9.html)
- **Preacher's Homiletical:** "Preserves them in their original places, marshals them as His hosts, sustains and directs their apparent motions through all the successive seasons of the year." [Preacher's Homiletical](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/job-9.html)

---

## v. 10: "He does great things beyond searching out, and wonders without number."

**Traditional reading:** Job echoes the words of Eliphaz from 5:9, showing he agrees with that much of his friends' theology. God's works in creation, providence, and grace cannot be fully searched out.

- **Gill:** "Great as to quantity and quality, not to be thoroughly searched out so as to tell their numbers, nor explain and express the nature of them to the full … The same things are said by Eliphaz … which Job here repeats, to show that he agreed with him." [Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/9.htm)
- **Preacher's Homiletical:** "In creation, His works wondrous and unsearchable, both in their multitude and magnitude, their complexity and minuteness. A drop of water … reveals millions of perfectly-formed living creatures." [Preacher's Homiletical](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/job-9.html)

---

## v. 11: "Were He to pass by me, I would not see Him; were He to move, I would not recognize Him."

**Traditional reading:** God is invisible and incomprehensible. His movements in providence are imperceptible to human senses — a major part of Job's agony was that God was acting on him but he could not perceive God's meaning or presence.

- **Gill:** "This is expressive of the invisibility of God … and of the imperceptibleness of his motions and of his works." [Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/9.htm)
- **Preacher's Homiletical:** "A great part of Job's trial, that while God was so painfully visiting him he was entirely in the dark as to His meaning." [Preacher's Homiletical](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/job-9.html)

---

## v. 12: "If He takes away, who can stop Him? Who dares to ask Him, 'What are You doing?'"

**Traditional reading:** God's sovereignty is absolute — no one can restrain His hand or demand an explanation from Him.

- **Geneva:** "He shows that when God executes his power, he does it justly, as no one can control him." [Geneva](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gsb/job-9.html)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** "Job saw God's power as if it were amoral, a sovereign freedom, an uncontrollable power that works mysteriously to do whatever he wills so that no one can stop him and ask, 'What are you doing?' (Smick)." [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-9/)

---

## v. 13: "God does not restrain His anger; the helpers of Rahab cower beneath Him."

**Traditional reading:** "Rahab" here is not the woman of Jericho but a poetic name for a mythical sea-monster or chaos-dragon, symbolising the proud forces opposed to God. Even the mightiest powers opposed to God ("helpers of Rahab") are crushed.

- **Nicoll (Expositor's Bible):** "The Almighty, he says, is like a lion that seizes the prey … a wrathful tyrant under whom the helpers of Rahab, those powers that according to some nature myth sustain the dragon of the sea in its conflict with heaven, stoop and give way." [Expositor's Bible](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/job-9.html)
- **Gill:** "Rahab … is a name of Egypt … and the helpers of Rahab are the inhabitants of Egypt … or the pride and haughtiness of men, which must stoop under the mighty hand of God." [Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/9.htm) [Gill discusses Rahab at length; the excerpt cuts off but indicates the traditional identifications.]

---

## vv. 14–15: "How then can I answer Him or choose my arguments against Him? For even if I were right, I could not answer. I could only beg my Judge for mercy."

**Traditional reading:** Given God's overwhelming power, Job concludes he cannot argue his case. Even if he were actually innocent (as he believes he is), he could not win a legal contest with God. His only recourse would be to plead for mercy — not to demand justice.

- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** "How then can I answer Him: Job's problem is clear; he understood that God is righteous and mighty; what he can't understand is how God will use that righteousness or might to help him." [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-9/)
- **Geneva:** "Meaning, in his own opinion, signifying that man will sometimes flatter himself to be righteous which before God is an abomination." [Geneva](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gsb/job-9.html)
- **Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary:** "He would instead make a respectful supplication or appeal for mercy, help, or compassion, as an accused before a judge." [Garner-Howes](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/job-9.html)

---

## vv. 16–17: "If I summoned Him and He answered me, I do not believe He would listen to my voice. For He would crush me with a tempest and multiply my wounds without cause."

**Traditional reading:** Even if God did respond to Job's summons, Job believes God would not give him a fair hearing. God would simply overwhelm him with more suffering. "Without cause" is Job's anguished assertion of his relative innocence — he has done nothing to deserve this.

- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** "He crushes me with a tempest, and multiplies my wounds without cause: Job felt that God's might was against him, not for him." [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-9/)
- **Geneva:** "I am not able to feel my sins so great, as I feel the weight of his plagues; and this he speaks to condemn his dullness and to justify God." [Geneva](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gsb/job-9.html)

---

## v. 18: "He does not let me catch my breath, but overwhelms me with bitterness."

**Traditional reading:** Job's afflictions are relentless — he has no respite, no moment to recover. The "bitterness" (Hebrew *mamrorim*, "bitter things") fills his life.

- **Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary:** "The Lord will not permit him to breathe, get his breath, swallow his spittle, except he do it with bitterness, suffering, and pain." [Garner-Howes](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/job-9.html)

---

## vv. 19–20: "If it is a matter of strength, He is indeed mighty! If it is a matter of justice, who can summon Him? Even if I were righteous, my mouth would condemn me; if I were blameless, it would declare me guilty."

**Traditional reading:** In strength, God wins absolutely. In justice, no one can compel God to appear in court. Job then makes a striking statement: if he claimed to be righteous, his very act of self-justification would condemn him — it would prove him arrogant and perverse.

**— Spurgeon (Baptist):** Spurgeon preached a sermon titled "A Blow at Self-Righteousness" on this verse. He told the story of an old man in Wiltshire who claimed he had never done anything wrong: "'But,' said someone to him, 'you are a sinner, you know.' 'I know I ain't,' he said. 'Well, but God says that you are.' … He said, 'God may say what he likes, but I know I ain't.' So, you see, he even contradicted God himself, and is not that a great sin for anybody to commit?" (Quoted in Enduring Word.) [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-9/) / [Spurgeon's Verse Expositions](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/job-9.html)

- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** "If he were to proclaim his own righteousness, the words themselves would be evidence of enough pride and arrogance to condemn him … Job 9:20 says that if a man justifies himself, his own mouth will condemn him. Romans 8:33-34 tells us that if God justifies a man, then none can condemn him." [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-9/)
- **Geneva:** "If I stood in my own defence yet God would have just cause to condemn me if he examined my heart and conscience." [Geneva](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gsb/job-9.html)
- **Garner-Howes Baptist:** "Job … does not consider himself to be perfect, nor would he dare contend such in a court of Divine equity … Should he attempt such he asserted that he would find his own mouth entrapping, betraying, or condemning him." [Garner-Howes](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/job-9.html)

---

## vv. 21–22: "Though I am blameless, I have no concern for myself; I despise my own life. It is all the same, and so I say, 'He destroys both the blameless and the wicked.'"

**Traditional reading:** Job reaches a dark conclusion: God destroys both innocent and guilty alike. This is a direct contradiction of Bildad's claim that the blameless never perish (Job 8:20). Job is "blameless" (*tam*) in the relative sense (as God Himself declared in 1:1, 1:8), not claiming sinlessness. His despair leads him to say life has become worthless to him.

- **Geneva:** "If God punishes according to his justice, he will destroy them who are counted perfect as well as them that are wicked." [Geneva](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gsb/job-9.html)
- **Constable:** "Job came to the point of concluding that it did not matter whether he was innocent since God destroys both the guiltless, like himself, and the wicked (Job 9:22)." [Constable](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/job-9.html)
- **Nicoll (Expositor's Bible):** "God would assail his life. Job replies in fierce revolt, 'Assail it, take it away, I care not, for I despise it. Whether one is righteous or evil, it is all the same. God destroys the perfect and the wicked.'" [Expositor's Bible](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/job-9.html)
- **Garner-Howes Baptist:** "God destroys or brings to great suffering and loss both the perfect (upright and mature) and the wicked, as the law of sin and death strikes the good and the bad … Great suffering does not prove great personal sin, else Jesus would not have so suffered." [Garner-Howes](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/job-9.html)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** "'So the sense is, Though God should give sentence for me, yet I should be so overwhelmed with the dread and terror of the Divine Majesty, that I should be weary of my life' (Poole)." [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-9/)

---

## v. 23: "When the scourge brings sudden death, He mocks the despair of the innocent."

**Traditional reading:** One of the most difficult verses in Job. In Job's anguished perception, when disaster (plague, lightning, accident) kills suddenly, God seems to laugh at the anguish of the innocent. This is not doctrine — it is Job's honest, tortured cry from his experience.

- **Ellicott:** "The scourge slay suddenly — Probably meaning that in the case of hidden calamity overtaking an innocent man, He, God, will laugh at it: that is to say, take no more notice of it than if it furnished Him with sport." [Ellicott](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/job-9.html)
- **Nicoll (Expositor's Bible):** "If a scourge such as lightning, accident, or disease slayeth suddenly, there seems to be nothing but mockery of the innocent. God looks down on the wreck of human hope, from the calm sky after the thunderstorm." [Expositor's Bible](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/job-9.html)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** "Job felt that not only was God distant and silent, but He was also having sport at the expense of godly sufferers like Job." Guzik adds Spurgeon's pastoral note: "As one is startled by a shriek, or saddened by a groan, so these sharp utterances of Job astonish us at first, and then awake our pity." [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-9/)
- **Garner-Howes Baptist (softening the verse):** "When the Lord slays or scourges the wicked suddenly, the innocent too may 'pine away' … as God laughs at the trial (testing) of the innocent, knowing that he is working eventual joy and happiness and triumph for the life of that person." [Garner-Howes](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/job-9.html)

---

## v. 24: "The earth is given into the hand of the wicked; He blindfolds its judges. If it is not He, then who is it?"

**Traditional reading:** Job observes empirically that in this fallen world the wicked often prosper and judges are blinded to justice. Since God is sovereign, Job traces this ultimately to God's permissive will. The verse is a sharp challenge: if God is not responsible for this state of affairs, then who is?

- **Geneva:** "That they cannot see to do justice … That can show the contrary?" [Geneva](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gsb/job-9.html)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** "Clarke on the earth is given into the hands of the wicked: 'Is it not most evident that the worst men possess most of this world's goods, and that the righteous are scarcely ever in power or affluence? This was the case in Job's time; it is the case still. Therefore prosperity and adversity in this life are no marks either of God's approbation or disapprobation.'" [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-9/)
- **Constable:** "Further evidences of His injustice include the facts that innocent people die in plagues (Job 9:23) and the wicked prosper in the earth (Job 9:24)." [Constable](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/job-9.html)
- **Nicoll (Expositor's Bible):** "And in the world of men the wicked have their way. God veils the face of the judge so that he is blinded to the equity of the cause. Thus, after the arguments of his friends, Job is compelled to see wrong everywhere, and to say that it is the doing of God. The strophe ends with the abrupt fierce demand, —If not, who then is it?" [Expositor's Bible](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/job-9.html)

---

## vv. 25–26: "My days are swifter than a runner; they flee without seeing good. They sweep by like boats of papyrus, like an eagle swooping down on its prey."

**Traditional reading:** Job laments the speed of his life. He uses three vivid images: a swift runner (courier), reed-boats (light skiffs on the Nile), and an eagle diving for prey. His life is not only swift but hostile — it "swoops" on him like a predator. He sees no "good" (prosperity, happiness) in his fleeting days.

- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** "Job felt that his life was spinning and running completely out of control. Time moved fast and was like a hostile predator against him (like an eagle swooping on its prey)." [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-9/)
- **Garner-Howes Baptist:** "He compares the brevity of life with the news carriers of the day, the fastest mode of carrying royal messages on dromedaries or by fast running footmen … like a swift sailing ship, ships of Ebeh, made of papyrus reed, sailed on the Nile river in Egypt." [Garner-Howes](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/job-9.html)

---

## vv. 27–28: "If I were to say, 'I will forget my complaint and change my expression and smile,' I would still dread all my sufferings; I know that You will not acquit me."

**Traditional reading:** Job cannot simply decide to cheer up. Even if he tried to put on a brave face, his dread would remain because he feels God has already condemned him. The shift to "You" (direct address to God) is sudden and personal.

- **Geneva:** "I think not to fall into these afflictions, but my sorrows bring me to these manifold infirmities, and my conscience condemns me." [Geneva](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gsb/job-9.html)
- **Garner-Howes Baptist:** "If he should leave off all his complaining … he would still fear all his sorrows that had befallen him, and that God would not hold him to be innocent of a need for the trials that had been brought on him by Satan." [Garner-Howes](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/job-9.html)

---

## vv. 29–31: "Since I am already found guilty, why should I labor in vain? If I should wash myself with snow and cleanse my hands with lye, then You would plunge me into the pit, and even my own clothes would despise me."

**Traditional reading:** Job feels condemned no matter what. Even if he used the purest cleansing agents — snow-water (considered exceptionally pure) and lye (a strong alkali soap) — God would simply throw him back into the mire. The image is vivid: he becomes so loathsome that even his own clothes would recoil from his diseased body.

**— Spurgeon (Baptist):** Spurgeon saw the washing with snow-water as a picture of the vain things sinners do to justify themselves: snow-water is hard to get (precious), reputed for purity, and comes from heaven not earth (seemingly more "spiritual") — yet it cannot cleanse sin. Of "my own clothes shall abhor me," Spurgeon said: "When the Lord, the Holy Spirit, convinces a man of sin, the words of Job are none too strong … you must be dirty indeed when your very clothes seem ashamed to hang upon you." [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-9/) / [Spurgeon](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/job-9.html)

- **Geneva:** "Though I seem pure in my own eyes, yet all is but corruption before God … Whatever I would use to cover my filthiness with, it would disclose me even more." [Geneva](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gsb/job-9.html)
- **Garner-Howes Baptist:** "He realized that he had no self-righteousness that would commend him to God." [Garner-Howes](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/job-9.html)

---

## vv. 32–33: "For He is not a man like me, that I can answer Him, that we can take each other to court. Nor is there a mediator between us, to lay his hand upon us both."

**Traditional reading: The central cry of the chapter.** Job recognises the fundamental inequality: God is not a human being who can be summoned to court. The solution would be a "daysman" (KJV) — an arbitrator, mediator, or umpire — who could lay his hand authoritatively on both parties, bridging the gap. Job feels this is impossible, yet his longing points directly to Christ.

- **Pulpit Commentary:** "On one of two conditions only, Job thinks, could the contest be even between himself and God. (1) If God, divesting himself of all his Divine attributes, became man; (2) if some third man could be found, some umpire or arbitrator … The Christian scheme … provides almost a literal fulfilment of both conditions, since the God who is to judge us is 'true Man,' and is also a Mediator, or 'Third-man,' between us and the offended Father." [Pulpit](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/9.htm)
- **Ellicott:** "Is not that confession, if we believe that such a daysman as Job longed for has been given, itself a witness that it came from God? … We know that a daysman has laid his hand upon us both; and while we see that this is what Job wanted, we cannot but see more plainly that this is what we want." [Ellicott](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/9.htm)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** "Job needed someone to sort out the differences between him and God … 'Here, then, was Job crying out for some one who could stand authoritatively between God and himself, and so create a way of meeting, a possibility of contact' (Morgan). … What Job longed for is fulfilled in Jesus. He fulfills all the qualifications for a mediator." [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-9/)
- **James Smith (Precept Austin):** "These well-known words truthfully express the deepest need of a sinful suffering spirit. O for one capable to act as umpire between a mighty God and a miserable soul … This great need has been perfectly met in Jesus Christ for, 'If any man sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous.'" [Smith](https://www.preceptaustin.org/job-commentary-james-smith)
- **Nicoll (Expositor's Bible):** "There is no daysman between us … The idea of a daysman, although the possibility of such a friendly helper is denied, is a new mark of boldness in the thought of the drama. In that one word the inspired writer strikes the note of a Divine purpose which he does not yet foresee. We must not say that here we have the prediction of a Redeemer at once God and man. The author has no such affirmation to make. But very remarkably the desires of Job are led forth in that direction in which the advent and work of Christ have fulfilled the decree of grace." [Expositor's Bible](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/job-9.html)
- **Garner-Howes Baptist:** "There was no daysman, arbitrator, mediator, or umpire between Job and God to lay his hand on both … But in matters of offense there is for us a mediator, even Jesus Christ, our advocate, mediator and intercessor." [Garner-Howes](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/job-9.html)
- **Pulpit (on "daysman"):** "Literally 'judge or arbitrator' called a 'daysman,' since he appoints the day on which the arbitration is to come off. The LXX renders by μεσίτης, 'mediator.'" [Pulpit](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/9.htm)
- **Geneva:** "Who might make an accord between God and me, speaking of impatience, and yet confessing God to be just in punishing him." [Geneva](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gsb/job-9.html)

## v. 34: "Let Him remove His rod from me, so that His terror will no longer frighten me."

**Traditional reading:** Job wishes for the removal of God's "rod" — the instrument of his affliction — and the terror of God's overwhelming majesty. This would be part of the mediator's role: to create conditions where a fair hearing is possible.

- **Pulpit:** "Job means that it would be a part of the duty of the 'daysman' to see that God's rod was removed from him before he was called upon to plead, so that he might not labour under so great a disadvantage as his sufferings would place him under." [Pulpit](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/9.htm)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** "As shebet signifies, not only rod, but also scepter or the ensign of royalty, Job might here refer to God sitting in his majesty upon the judgment-seat; and this sight so appalled him, that, filled with terror, he was unable to speak (Clarke)." [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-9/)
- **Garner-Howes Baptist:** "Job appealed for God to 'remove the rod,' or take away the affliction Satan had laid upon him, to terrify him. He seems to know that Satan had inflicted grief and anxiety, though God had permitted it, and God alone could remove the pain and sorrow." [Garner-Howes](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/job-9.html)

## v. 35: "Then I would speak without fear of Him. But as it is, I am on my own."

**Traditional reading:** The BSB rendering "I am on my own" reflects the difficulty of the Hebrew. The literal Hebrew is difficult: "I am not so with myself" or "It is not so with me." Various interpretations:

- **Ellicott:** "Literally, I am not so with me. The words are variously understood: 'It is not so with me,' i.e., 'I am not thus without fear' … or, 'I am not so as ye suppose,' i.e., guilty, but innocent; or, 'Am I not right with myself?' i.e., inwardly conscious of my integrity and innocence (Job 10:1)." [Ellicott](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/9.htm)
- **Pulpit:** "I am not in such a position as to enter on my justification. I am weighted by my sufferings." [Pulpit](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/9.htm)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** "Because he lacked a mediator, Job felt that he could not speak with God. 'I am not free from his terror, and therefore cannot and dare not plead my case boldly with him' (Poole)." [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-9/)
- **Constable:** "'I am not like that in myself' (Job 9:35) means 'that is not the way it is with regard to my case' (Zuck)." [Constable](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/job-9.html)

## Tradition-Specific Notes

### Reformed / Presbyterian
The sources did not yield a specifically Reformed commentary from ligonier.org or monergism.com dedicated to Job 9. However, the general Reformed emphasis on God's sovereignty and human inability is woven throughout the traditional commentaries. Constable (Dallas Theological Seminary) notes: "Job's first address to Bildad was a magnificent confession of the sovereignty of God… Yet Job's recognition of God's sovereignty is more fatalistic than grounded in the nature of God as a just and righteous One." [Constable](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/job-9.html)

### Baptist
- **Spurgeon:** Preached on v. 20 ("A Blow at Self-Righteousness") and vv. 30–31 (on the folly of self-cleansing). Emphasises that self-justification is self-condemnation, and that only Christ's righteousness can justify a sinner. [Spurgeon's Expositions](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/job-9.html) / [Enduring Word summary](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-9/)
- **Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary:** Emphasises that Job's suffering was from Satan by divine permission, not from God directly; that v. 22 refutes the friends' simplistic retribution theology; and that the mediator of v. 33 is fulfilled in Christ. [Garner-Howes](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/job-9.html)

### Pentecostal / Charismatic
- **Enduring Word (David Guzik):** Guzik's commentary connects the chapter extensively to Jesus — noting how Job's description of God (treading on waves, creating stars, doing wonders) "unknowingly paints an accurate portrait of Jesus." He makes an extended application about the Mediator being fulfilled in Christ, who meets all four qualifications of a mediator. [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-9/)

### Anglican (older commentaries)
- **Ellicott's Commentary for English Readers:** A classic Anglican work (1878). Ellicott draws out the Christological significance of vv. 32–33 and notes the astronomy in v. 9 as evidence of the writer's era. [Ellicott](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/9.htm)

### Methodist / Wesleyan, Lutheran, Catholic, Orthodox
Due to search/fetch limits, specific pages from wesley.nnu.edu, seedbed.com, lcms.org, 1517.org, newadvent.org, catholic.com, and oca.org could not be retrieved. The material above from broadly evangelical and older Anglican/Puritan sources represents the majority Protestant reading.

### Modern Scholarship
Due to search/fetch limits, pages from bibleodyssey.org and netbible.org could not be retrieved. However, Constable notes: "In the ancient Near East this arbitrator was a judge whose verdict was more often a settlement proposal that the litigants could either accept or reject" — a historical insight on vv. 32–33. [Constable](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/job-9.html). The Expositor's Bible (Nicoll) also notes the "nature myth" background of Rahab in v. 13. [Expositor's Bible](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/job-9.html)

## Summary of Cross-Tradition Agreements and Differences

| Topic | Agreement | Differences |
|---|---|---|
| **v. 2 — "How can man be just with God?"** | All agree it is the fundamental question of justification. | Constable (DTS/dispensational) says it's about vindication, not salvation. Gill (Reformed Baptist) and Pulpit (Anglican) see it pointing to imputed righteousness through Christ. |
| **vv. 22–24 — God destroys both blameless and wicked** | All agree this is Job's anguished, limited perspective — not doctrinal error but honest expression. | Garner-Howes (Baptist) softens v. 23 by interpreting "laughs" as God knowing eventual triumph for the righteous. Nicoll (Expositor's) treats it as Job's near-blasphemous revolt. |
| **vv. 32–33 — The mediator/daysman** | All Christian traditions see Christ as the fulfilment. | Nicoll (Expositor's) cautions against reading it as direct prediction: "We must not say that here we have the prediction of a Redeemer at once God and man. The author has no such affirmation to make." Yet all still see it as divinely orchestrated longing. |
| **v. 13 — "Rahab"** | Traditionally identified as Egypt or a chaos-monster. | Gill lists both options. Nicoll notes the "nature myth" background. |
| **v. 35 — "I am on my own"** | All note the Hebrew is difficult. | Ellicott lists three possible interpretations (see above). |
